SUMMARY 
This report recommends that City Council state its intention to designate the property at 
66 Gerrard Street East (including entrance addresses at 366, 368, and 370 Church 
Street and 64 Gerrard Street East) under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act 
for its cultural heritage value according to the Statement of Significance which includes 
a description of heritage attributes found in Attachment 1. 
The subject property at 66 Gerrard Street East is located on the north side of Gerrard 
Street East, at the northwest corner of Church Street, within the Downtown Yonge East 
neighbourhood of downtown Toronto. 
A location map and current photograph of the heritage property are included in 
Attachment 2. 
Constructed circa 1855, the property comprises a row of three attached brick house-
form buildings, historically known as 62, 64, and 66 Gerrard Street East, designed in the 
Georgian architectural style and raised to two-and-a-half storeys c. 1875 with a Second 
Empire mansard roof spanning the three units, together with a c. 1910 rear addition 
forming a streetwall along Church Street. The property forms part of the historic context 
of the Gerrard and Church Street area, at the southern edge of the present-day Church 
and Wellesley neighbourhood. 
The subject property at 66 Gerrard Street East was listed on the City of Toronto's 
Heritage Register on November 6, 1974. 
This property is one of eighteen pre-1870 listed properties citywide which have been 
identified as candidates for designation through the City's implementation of Bill 23 
amendments to the Ontario Heritage Act and its ongoing prioritization strategy for listed 
properties that must be designated or removed from the Heritage Register by January 
1, 2027.

POLICY AND REGULATION CONSIDERATIONS 
Provincial Plans and Policies 
The conservation of cultural heritage resources is an integral component of good 
planning, contributing to a sense of place, economic prosperity, and healthy and 
equitable communities. Heritage conservation in Ontario is identified as a provincial 
interest under the Planning Act. https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90p13 
Further, the policies and definitions of the Provincial Planning Statement (2024) identify 
the Ontario Heritage Act as the primary legislation through which heritage evaluation 
and heritage conservation will be implemented. 
Provincial Planning Statement, 2024 (ontario.ca) 
Ontario Regulation 9/06 sets out the criteria for evaluating properties to be designated 
under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act. The criteria are based on an 
evaluation of design/physical value, historical and associative value and contextual 
value.  A property may be designated under Section 29 of the Act if it meets two or 
more of the provincial criteria for determining whether it is of cultural heritage value or 
interest.

STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE 
(REASONS FOR DESIGNATION) 
The property at 66 Gerrard Street East (including entrance addresses at 366, 368, and 
370 Church Street and 64 Gerrard Street East) is worthy of designation under Part IV, 
Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act for its cultural heritage value and meets Ontario 
Regulation 9/06, the provincial criteria prescribed for municipal designation. 
Description 
The subject property at 66 Gerrard Street East (including entrance addresses at 366, 
368, and 370 Church Street and 64 Gerrard Street East) is located on the north side of 
Gerrard Street East, at the northwest corner of Church Street, within the Downtown 
Yonge East neighbourhood of downtown Toronto. Constructed circa 1855, the property 
comprises a row of three attached brick house-form buildings, historically known as 62, 
64, and 66 Gerrard Street East, designed in the Georgian architectural style and raised 
to two-and-a-half storeys circa 1875 with a Second Empire mansard roof spanning the 
three units, together with a rear addition of circa 1910 forming a streetwall along Church 
Street. The property forms part of the historic context of the Gerrard and Church Street 
area, at the southern edge of the present-day Church and Wellesley community. 
Statement of Cultural Heritage Value 
Design and Physical Value 
The property at 66 Gerrard Street East has design and physical value as a 
representative example of a rowhouse designed in the Georgian architectural style, with 
later alterations in the Second Empire style. The Georgian style was commonly applied 
to rowhouses constructed in Toronto through the 1850s and 1860s and is classically 
derived, emphasizing symmetry, proportion, and restrained ornamentation. The Second 
Empire style, popular in Toronto through the 1860s and 1870s, was applied to 
institutional and government buildings, as well as detached villas and rowhouses; 
features representative of the style include the mansard roof and dormer windows. At 
66 Gerrard Street East, the original circa 1855 row of three attached Georgian dwellings 
was raised circa 1875 by the addition of a mansard roof, thereby introducing Second 
Empire features. The distinct entrances to each rowhouse were removed in the early-
20th century, coinciding with the property's conversion into a single commercial building 
with a primary entrance fronting onto Gerrard Street East. 
The subject property displays the characteristics of the Georgian style through its row of 
three uniform, attached, house-form units clad in buff (yellow) brick and with rectangular 
window openings with stone sills and lintels arranged in a regular composition on the 
primary (south) façade. The Second Empire alteration is expressed through the 
mansard roof spanning the three units, clad in slate on the primary (south) façade and 
articulated by two gabled dormers set within each bay: the central bay containing single 
rectangular windows with sunburst panels in the gable ends, and the flanking bays 
containing paired dormers with pedimented gables. Further characteristic detailing on 
the primary façade includes the buff brick string course with cross detailing separating 
66 Gerrard Street East - Notice of Intention to Designate Page 6 of 30

the first and second storeys, the sawtooth and dentillated brick coursing defining the top 
of the second storey, and the metal cornice above. The circa 1910 rear addition forming 
a streetwall along Church Street continues the Second Empire form and styling of the 
row, with the facade clad in buff brick and with its own mansard roof with flat-roofed 
dormers, a metal cornice, and a stepped gable end wall at the rear. 
Historical and Associative Value 
The property at 66 Gerrard Street East has historical and associative value due to its 
direct associations with a person and businesses that are significant to Toronto’s 
LGBTQ+ community. In 1978, 64 Gerrard Street East became home to Crispin’s, a 
restaurant known as a place where gay men and women could feel comfortable and 
were welcomed; in the lower level was Buddy’s Backroom Bar, a gay bar. Hancock 
Simpson Architects were commissioned for the commercial conversion work, which 
included the addition of two new entrances, one for Crispin's on the south (front) 
elevation, and another on the north (rear) elevation for Buddy's Back Room Bar. Both 
were associated with the prominent gay activist George Hislop (1927–2005) and his 
partner Ron Shearer. Buddy’s is recognized as part of the shift of Toronto’s gay scene 
from Yonge Street to Church Street in the mid-to-late 1970s, and as an establishment 
that fostered community, conversation, and organizing. 
The same lower-level space at 64 Gerrard Street East subsequently operated as the 
Lizard Lounge and, later as The Bijou, an adult venue whose patrons were subject to a 
series of police raids in the summer of 1999 that prompted the formation of the June 13 
Committee. The property later became home to the Hassle Free Clinic, a local sexual-
health clinic that has provided essential health care for members of Toronto’s LGBTQ+ 
community since the 1970s. Through these associations, the property reflects and 
documents the development of Toronto’s LGBTQ+ community at the southern edge of 
the Church and Wellesley neighbourhood. 
The property at 66 Gerrard Street East has historical and associative value due to its 
ability to yield information contributing to an understanding of Toronto’s LGBTQ+ 
community. As one of the earliest venues to cater towards the gay community east of 
Yonge Street towards Church Street, and as the site of one of the last bath house raids, 
66 Gerrard Street East has the potential to yield information on the establishment of The 
Village, and early efforts to establish businesses that publicly catered to the community. 
Contextual Value 
The property at 66 Gerrard Street East has contextual value as it is important in 
defining, maintaining, and supporting the historic character of the Gerrard and Church 
Street area. The subject property forms part of a collection of mid- to late-19th-century 
house-form buildings around the intersection of Church and Gerrard Streets that 
together maintain a fine-grained, pedestrian-scaled, streetscape characteristic of the 
19th-century neighbourhood. Anchoring the northwest corner of Church and Gerrard, 
the property supports this historic character amid the taller, later development that has 
replaced much of the surrounding fabric.

The property also has contextual value as it is physically, visually, and historically linked 
to its surroundings. It stands among a group of surviving mid- to late-19th-century 
house-form buildings in the immediate area, including 70 Gerrard Street East (circa 
1845); 74 Gerrard Street East (1885); 76 and 78 Gerrard Street East (1858); 322 
Church Street (1847); and 418 Church Street (1891). The property is historically linked 
to the medical and institutional character that developed along Gerrard Street East in 
the second half of the 19th century and, through the businesses it hosted during the 
second half of the 20th century to the development of Toronto’s LGBTQ+ community 
and the Church-Wellesley village, at whose southern edge it stands. Through its siting 
and long-standing presence at the corner of Church and Gerrard Streets, the subject 
property is historically and visually linked to this established setting.

3. RESEARCH 
This section of the report describes the history, architecture and context of the property. 
Visual resources related to the research are located in Section 4. Archival and 
contemporary sources for the research are found in Section 5 (List of Sources). 
Indigenous Communities 
For time immemorial, Toronto has been home to Indigenous peoples. Ojibway oral 
histories speak of Ice People, who lived at a time when ice covered the land.1 Following 
the retreat of glaciers approximately 13,000 years ago, small groups of Indigenous 
peoples moved from place to place, hunting and gathering the food they needed 
according to the seasons. Over millennia, they adapted to dramatically changing 
environmental conditions, developing and acquiring new technologies as they did 
so. Waterways and the lake were vital sources of fresh water and nourishment, and 
shorelines and nearby areas were important sites for gathering, trading, hunting, fishing, 
and ceremonies. Long-distance trade moved valuable resources across the land. 
After maize and squash were introduced to Southern Ontario, by approximately 500 CE, 
horticulture began to supplement food sources. By 1300 CE, villages focused on 
growing food became year-round settlements surrounded by crops. These villages were 
home to ancestors of the Huron-Wendat Nation, who would continue to occupy 
increasingly larger villages in the Toronto area and beyond. These villages were 
connected to well-established travel routes which were part of local and long-distance 
trail networks, including the Carrying Place trails on the Don, Rouge and Humber rivers 
that connected Lake Ontario to Georgian Bay. Beads made from seashells from the 
eastern seaboard were found at the Alexandra site in North York, which was a 
community of 800-1000 people in approximately 1350. 
By 1600, the Wendat had formed a confederation of individual nations, and had 
concentrated most of their villages away from Lake Ontario, in the Georgian Bay area. 
Following contact with French explorers and missionaries in Southern Ontario in the 
early 1600s, European diseases decimated First Nations. Competition for furs to trade 
with Europeans and the desire to replenish numbers through absorption of captives, 
among other factors2, contributed to the Beaver Wars, which after 1640, saw the 
Haudenosaunee Confederacy expand into Southern Ontario, dispersing the Wendat. 
Within the boundaries of today's Toronto, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy then 
occupied villages on the Carrying Place trails on the Humber and Rouge Rivers from 
approximately the 1660s to the 1680s. 
In the late 1680s, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy chose to leave their village in the 
Toronto area and returned to their homelands in upstate New York. As evidenced by the 
1701 Great Peace of Montreal, the 1701 Nanfan Treaty, and the Dish with One Spoon 
Treaty, the Haudenosaunee continued to have an interest in the resources of the area.

Anishinaabe people from the Lake Superior region then moved into the Toronto area. 
While the Wendat and Haudenosaunee people lived in year-round villages surrounded 
by crops, the Anishinaabe people continued to live primarily by seasonally moving 
across the land to hunt, fish and gather resources that were available at a specific time, 
including migrating birds and maple syrup. To the west of Toronto, the Anishinaabe 
people became known as the Mississaugas of the Credit. To the east, they became 
known as the Chippewas of Beausoleil, Georgina Island and Rama and the 
Mississaugas of Alderville, Curve Lake, Hiawatha, Scugog Island.3 
In 1787, as the British began to prepare for an influx of colonists into the area following 
the American Revolution, the British Crown negotiated the Toronto Purchase with the 
Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation to obtain title to the land. The flawed and poorly 
documented agreement was invalidated, and Treaty 13 was negotiated in 1805 for 
lands now including much of the City of Toronto. In 1923, the Governments of Ontario 
and Canada signed the Williams Treaties for over 20,000 km2, including portions of 
eastern Toronto, with seven First Nations of the Chippewa of Lake Simcoe (Beausoleil, 
Georgina Island and Rama) and the Mississauga of the north shore of Lake Ontario 
(Alderville, Curve Lake, Hiawatha and Scugog Island). 
The Mississaugas, Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee, or the Wendat did not traditionally 
regard land as a commodity to be sold. Following the Toronto Purchase, the British 
government quickly set out to survey the land into lots which were either sold or granted 
into private ownership of settlers. In 2010, the Government of Canada settled the 
Toronto Purchase Claim with the Mississaugas of the Credit after agreeing that the 
Mississaugas were originally unfairly compensated. In 2018, the Williams Treaties First 
Nations settled litigation about land surrenders and harvesting rights with the 
Governments of Canada and Ontario. 
The City of Toronto remains the traditional territory of many nations including the 
Mississaugas of the Credit, the Anishnabeg, the Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee and 
the Wendat peoples and is now home to many diverse First Nations, Inuit and Métis 
peoples. Toronto is also covered by Treaty 13 signed with the Mississaugas of the 
Credit, and the Williams Treaties signed with seven Mississaugas and Chippewa First 
Nations. 
i. HISTORICAL INFORMATION 
The following section outlines the history and facts related to the properties which are 
the basis for determining historical or associative value of Criteria 4, 5 or 6 according to 
O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
Park Lot 7 
In 1793, Park Lot 7 was granted to the British military officer Captain John McGill (1752-
1834). McGill had previously served under John Graves Simcoe in the American 
Revolutionary War, after which he settled in Upper Canada before arriving in York

(Toronto) where he was appointed to the Legislative Council in 1797 and as Lieutenant 
of the County of York in 1805.4 In 1803, McGill constructed a house on Park Lot 7 
looking south to Queen Street East, south of present-day Shuter Street. 
McGill died in 1834, and, owing to his lack of a direct heir, his estate was inherited by 
his nephew, Peter McCutcheon, on the condition that McCutcheon would assume the 
surname McGill. McCutcheon was at that time a merchant newly appointed to the 
position of President of the Bank of Montreal; it was from his seat in Montreal that he 
proceeded to sell-off the lands still held within Park Lot 7. In 1836, a Plan of Subdivision 
was filed encompassing land from Lot Street (Queen Street East) to Gerrard Street East 
and from Yonge Street to Jarvis Street, maintaining McGill Cottage and Garden on the 
land occupied today by Metropolitan United Church, and establishing something close 
to the contemporary street pattern (Figure 4). 
62, 64, and 66 Gerrard Street East 
The subject property at 66 Gerrard Street East comprises three brick townhouses, 
historically known as 62, 64, and 66 Gerrard Street East, and is located on the 
northwest corner of Church Street and Gerrard Street East. The property includes Lot 
17 and part of Lot 16 Plan 22A, which are shown on the 1836 Plan of Subdivision 
(Figure 4). 
In 1844, Lot 17 was sold by Peter McGill to Robert Moody; along with portions of Lot 16, 
the lands containing the subject properties transacted multiple times before being sold 
to William R. Graham in 1852. The addresses first appear in the City of Toronto 
directories in 1856; 62 Gerrard Street East is recorded as the home of Maurice Scollard, 
with 64 and 66 unoccupied. In 1858, three 2-storey brick dwellings are shown on 
Boulton’s Atlas of the City of Toronto and Vicinity (Figure 5), and the directory for 1859 
lists the occupants as William Ross (#62); R. C. Fitzgerald, teller (#64); and Charles 
Williamson, vinegar-maker (#66). 
The Graham family owned the three properties until 1880 and operated them as owner-
landlords; city directories show a variety of middle-class professionals living in the 
premises during this period. Around 1875, the mansard roof spanning all three 
townhouses was constructed,5 adding a half-storey as reflected in the 1880 Goad’s 
Atlas (Figure 6). 
In 1880, #66 was sold by the Graham family to Charles Sheard (1857-1929).6 Sheard 
was a Toronto-born doctor and son of the architect and Mayor of Toronto Joseph 
Sheard. He was educated at Trinity College, served as Toronto’s chief Medical Officer 
of Health from 1893 to 1910, and was elected a Member of Parliament for Toronto 
South from 1917 to 1925. Sheard’s tenure at #66 coincides with his early medical 
practice; in 1884 he married and moved to 314 Jarvis Street.

Sheard sold 66 Gerrard Street East to William Lloyd Wood, a druggist, in 1884. By this 
time the surrounding neighbourhood was well-developed, heavily influenced by the 
presence of the Toronto Normal School on the south side of Gerrard Street East, west 
of Church Street, alongside a variety of rowhouses, semi-detached, and detached 
homes. W. Lloyd Wood operated as a medical proprietor, or agent, for a range of 
medicinal companies, shown in the directories as the Lambert Pharmacal Company, 
Allen & Hanbury’s Ltd, and the H.K. Mulford Company. 
In 1856, the Toronto General Hospital was constructed on Gerrard Street East between 
Sackville and Sumach Streets in the Cabbagetown neighbourhood; in the years and 
decades that followed, the street and adjoining areas attracted a variety of medical 
schools, institutions, and practices. Notable area residents included Dr. Charles Sheard 
(314 Jarvis Street); one of the city’s first surgeons, Dr. Petros Constantinides (56 
Gerrard Street East); and the first Secretary of the Faculty of Medicine at the University 
of Toronto, Dr. Adam H. Wright (20 Gerrard Street East). 
It was during W. Lloyd Wood’s ownership that the three properties were combined and 
converted to commercial use; the 1910 Goad’s Atlas shows an extension to 66 Gerrard 
Street East extending north along Church Street, and between 1910 and 1912 Wood 
acquired 62 and 64 Gerrard Street East.7 
In 1922, following Wood’s death, the properties were transferred to a company (W. 
Lloyd Wood Ltd.). They were operated and held by the company until 1977 as a 
druggist’s and pharmacy. 
Following the sale of the property in 1977 to Fairway Construction Ltd., the building was 
leased to a range of tenants operating outside of the medical and pharmaceutical fields 
that had occupied the site for nearly a century. In 1978, 64 Gerrard Street East was 
leased to two establishments: Crispin’s, a dining establishment on the ground floor, and 
Buddy’s Backroom Bar, a gay bar that operated in the basement.8 Both were associated 
with the prominent gay activist George Hislop (1927-2005) and his partner, Ron 
Shearer. Alterations undertaken by Hancock Simpson Architects (Figures 12 & 13) 
including the current central primary entrance, and the creation of a front dining room 
and rear bar in the basement, with separate access to the bar from the rear alleyway. 
Crispin’s was one of a handful of restaurants that opened in proximity to Yonge Street 
and Church Street that was known to cater to Toronto’s gay community. The restaurant 
was featured in the January 1980 edition of The Body Politic as a gay eatery alongside 
a handful of similar establishments in the neighbourhood.9 Celebrated and 
acknowledged as a restaurant where gay men could feel comfortable, it was also 
recognized as serving so for a “…limited 'we': employed, urban, mostly men, almost all 
white…”10 The restaurant was described as comprising two dining rooms dressed as a

suburban ranch style living room, replete with end tables featuring large lamps and a

Crispin’s was advertised widely in both queer publications like The Body Politic and 
mainstream media: while The Globe and Mail’s Mary Walpole extolled its “charm and 
haute cuisine” appealing to the gallery and theatre crowd,11 The Body Politic 
encouraged patrons to drop in “next door” for a drink at Buddy’s (Figure 14). While 
Crispin’s was an establishment known for being gay-friendly, Buddy’s was a gay bar 
that explicitly catered to the community, advertised in community publications, and 
hosted gay-friendly events (Figure 15). Gay activist Rick Bebout described Buddy’s as 
marking a geographic shift in the gay scene as it moved from Yonge to Church Street, 
beginning in the mid-1970s with The Quest, Les Cavaliers, Jo Jo’s (later The Barn), and 
Buddy’s.12 Of note in Bebout’s recollection was Buddy’s characterization as a place that 
“…cultivated the one thing backrooms meant for sex never did: talk.”13 
The bar encouraged conversation, and at the entrance had a community bulletin board, 
uncommon in gay spaces at the time. It “became an institution, practically a community 
centre,”14 attracting a mix of men and women, older and younger, social and political. 
By 1987, Crispin’s and Buddy’s Backroom Bar had closed, and the space occupied by 
Buddy’s was re-cast as the Lizard Lounge, which advertised itself as “the only 
alternative social club” (Figure 17). The Lizard Lounge catered to Toronto’s progressive, 
alternative and fetish scene, hosting themed nights not exclusive or catering to the gay 
community (Figure 18). The Lizard Lounge was replaced by a venue called Dix by 1993. 
The Bijou, a gay adult venue, opened in the same lower-level space that had housed 
Buddy’s and the Lizard Lounge by 1996. In the summer of 1999, Toronto Police raided 
and arrested patrons of The Bijou: on June 13, two plainclothes officers charged 8 
patrons with indecency; on June 17, they served the owner, Craig Anderson, for a liquor 
violation and charged 4 more patrons; and on July 1, they returned to charge 7 more 
patrons.15 This pattern of intimidation echoed the Toronto Bathhouse Raids associated 
with Operation Soap in 1981, sparking editorializing in queer publications such as Xtra16 
decrying the raids, and in the conservative Toronto Sun. The events sparked the 
formation of the June 13 Committee, which sought to improve the relationship between 
police and the gay community, and led to the dropping of all charges.17

Since 2004/2005, a range of businesses have occupied the subject property, including 
the Hassle Free Clinic at 66 Gerrard Street East. The clinic was founded in February 
1973 on Yonge Street to serve the “drug-oriented street scene” and to provide STI and

the arrival of the AIDS crisis in 1983-84, the clinic provided essential services in 
anonymous testing, illegal in Ontario at the time, alongside promoting sexual health. 
The ribbon cutting marking the clinic’s opening at 66 Gerrard Street East was done by

ii.  ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION 
The following section provides an architectural description and analysis related to the 
property which will establish the basis for determining design or physical value of 
Criteria 1, 2 or 3 according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
The subject property at 66 Gerrard Street East, comprising the historic addresses of 62, 
64, and 66 Gerrard Street East, is a row of three attached brick house-form buildings, 
originally constructed c. 1855 as three two-storey dwellings on the north side of Gerrard 
Street East, west of Church Street. The original two storey dwellings were altered c. 
1875 with the addition of a half-storey mansard roof spanning the three rowhouses. A 
brick two-and-a-half-storey addition was constructed on the rear of 66 Gerrard Street 
East forming a streetwall on Church Street, north of Gerrard. The former residential 
entrances have been altered, with a single raised and recessed entrance in the centre 
unit providing access to the building. Three raised and recessed entrances on the 
Church Street addition provide additional access. 
The structure is clad in buff (yellow) brick on the first and second floors; the mansard 
roof on the Gerrard Street East primary façade is clad in slate shingles, while the 
mansard roof on the Church Street secondary façade is clad in asphalt shingles. The 
visible foundation on the primary façade is stone, except for the westernmost unit (#62) 
which is buff brick. Window openings on the first and second floors are rectangular with 
stone sills and lintels and are separated by a buff brick string course with cross 
detailing. Sawtooth and dentillated brick coursing defines the top of the second storey, 
with a metal cornice above. 
The mansard roof on the primary façade features two gabled dormer windows within 
each bay; the dormers within the centre bay contain single rectangular four pane 
windows with sunburst panels in the gable ends, while the flanking bays each contain 
two double window dormers with pedimented gables. 
The secondary façade on the original building is clad in buff brick on the first storey; the 
second and third storey facades have been parged and are punctuated by rectangular

iii. CONTEXT 
The following section provides contextual information and analysis related to the 
property which is the basis for determining contextual value of Criteria 7, 8 or 9 
according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
The City of Toronto Property Data Map attached (Attachment 2) shows the site of the 
property at 66 Gerrard Street East 
The subject property at 66 Gerrard Street East is located on the north side of Gerrard 
Street East at the northwest corner of Church Street, within the Downtown Yonge East 
neighbourhood. The land was subdivided from Park Lot 7 – the former estate of Captain 
John McGill – under the 1836 Plan of Subdivision and formed part of a residential 
district laid out in the mid-19th century and built up through the second half of the 
century with a mix of row, semi-detached, and detached houses, together with 
churches, schools and other institutions. 
The three attached brick dwellings historically known as 62, 64, and 66 Gerrard Street 
East form part of a collection of mid- to late- 19th century house-form buildings around 
the intersection of Church and Gerrard, including 70 Gerrard Street East (circa 1845, 
listed); 74 Gerrard Street East (1885, Part IV designated); 76 & 78 Gerrard Street East 
(1858, Part IV designated); 322 Church Street (1847, Part IV designated); and 418 
Church Street (1891, Part IV designated). Collectively, these properties maintain a fine-
grained, pedestrian-scaled streetscape that characterized the 19th-century 
neighbourhood, with 66 Gerrard Street East anchoring the northwest corner of Church 
and Gerrard amid the taller, later development that has replaced much of the 
surrounding historic fabric. 
The Church Street corridor became linked to the development of Toronto’s LGBTQ+ 
community in the later 20th century as it migrated from Yonge Street to Church and 
Wellesley. The subject property at 66 Gerrard Street East stands at the southern edge 
of the present-day Church and Wellesley community, historically hosting businesses 
associated with the gay community and continuing to do so to the present day. Today, 
the property reads as a physical record of the neighbourhood’s evolution from a mid-
Victorian residential enclave to a medical and commercial street, and, later, part of the 
city’s LGBTQ+ cultural geography.
